profile.name: Md Nazmul Islam
profile.role: Researcher in trustworthy and reliable AI
profile.headline: Building AI that is honest about what it knows
profile.tagline: Calibration, robustness and rigorous evaluation for deep learning, with applications in medical imaging.
profile.bio: I am a Computer Science and Engineering graduate of Rajshahi University of Engineering and Technology (RUET), Bangladesh. I study how far we can trust deep learning models. My work covers calibration and uncertainty, robustness to distribution shift, and careful evaluation. I apply these ideas to medical imaging, where a confident but wrong answer can cause real harm.
profile.contact: I am open to research collaborations and graduate study opportunities.

focus.statement: A model that is accurate but overconfident is not ready for the real world.
focus.body: I work on trustworthy and reliable AI. I test whether models stay reliable when the data changes, and whether the tools we use to measure trust can themselves be trusted. My main application area is medical imaging.

pillars.title: Calibration and uncertainty
pillars.text: Checking that a model's confidence matches how often it is right, and that it knows when to abstain.

pillars.title: Robustness to distribution shift
pillars.text: Measuring how models behave when data comes from new sources and conditions.

pillars.title: Rigorous evaluation
pillars.text: Pre-registered, multi-seed studies and leak-free data splits, so reported gains are real.

news.text: Joined St. Joseph International School as IT Officer.
Our paper on label noise in colorectal cancer classification was published in Applied Computational Intelligence and Soft Computing (Wiley).

research.title: Auditing Trustworthiness Evaluation in Medical Image Classification
points: Pre-registered, multi-seed audit of attention modules across 150 models and seven medical imaging datasets, testing accuracy, calibration and selective prediction.
Showed that standard post-hoc calibration fails under cross-site acquisition shift, and that slice-level splitting of a widely used CT benchmark inflates accuracy by 17.8 points.
